query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys designed for high-temperature applications, the ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer is governed by the preferential enrichment and controlled oxidation of selected alloying elements (e.g., Al and/or Cr). This enrichment leads to the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide (alumina and/or chromia) that slows further oxygen ingress and oxidation kinetics.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a complex, multi-element composition containing protective elements such as Al and Cr (e.g., compositions similar to AlCoCrFeNi or variants thereof), initially exhibiting a homogeneously distributed microstructure.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to high-temperature oxidizing conditions (air atmosphere) for a fixed duration, and compare with a control alloy variant that has a reduced content of the protective elements.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment (e.g., 850–1050 °C), controlled time exposures, and identical processing histories except for the targeted variation in protective element content.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent oxide layer (primarily alumina and/or chromia) forming at the alloy surface via preferential oxidation; the microstructural pathways (such as grain boundaries) facilitate the diffusion of the protective element to the surface.
generation.mechanism: Due to the chemical complexity intrinsic to HEAs, the kinetics of diffusion favor the selective migration and oxidation of protective elements. These elements form thermodynamically stable, slow-growing oxides that act as an oxygen diffusion barrier. The multi-element matrix minimizes rapid element depletion and prevents the formation of non-protective, porous oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA with enriched protective element content will exhibit a lower oxidation rate (lower weight gain, slower oxide growth) and a continuous, adherent, and chemically uniform protective oxide scale compared with the control HEA with reduced protective elements.
generation.baseline: Control HEA variants lacking the optimal concentration of protective elements (or having a coarser microstructure that hinders selective diffusion) which are expected to form less protective, more porous oxide scales and show higher oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for high-entropy alloys operating under high-temperature oxidation conditions (approximately 850–1050 °C) in oxidative atmospheres; its behavior might differ in environments with very high temperatures, reducing atmospheres, or in alloys missing the key protective elements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance and diffusion kinetics of the protective elements and the influence of microstructural factors (e.g., grain size, phase distribution) on oxide layer formation remain to be fully quantified. The relative contribution of each element (e.g., Al versus Cr) and potential interactions with minor constituents require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical processing and microstructural characteristics except that one set is enriched in the protective elements (e.g., higher Al and/or Cr content) while the other set has reduced amounts. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions (850–1050 °C) in air for an extended period. Monitor oxidation behavior using in situ XRD, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and surface analysis (e.g., XPS or SEM-EDS) to determine oxide phase composition and morphology.
measurements: Weight gain over time from TGA
Oxide scale thickness and continuity from cross-sectional SEM
Phase identification of oxide scales by XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sample enriched in protective elements does not form a continuous, adherent alumina/chromia scale and does not exhibit statistically lower oxidation rates (e.g., similar weight gains and oxide morphologies) compared to the control sample with lower protective element content, then the hypothesis that preferential enrichment governs the formation of a protective oxide layer is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
